messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: sort [for mixture components]
parts:
On 5/1/13 7:42 PM, Andrew Gelman wrote:
> B
> Do we have a sort() function or something similar in Stan?

No. There's an index of functions in the very back of
the manual.

It is on the to-do list of functions to add :-)

> I'm fitting a mixture model and thought it would be convenient to parameterize based
> on the ordering of the modes (i.e., redefining so that mu[1]<mu[2]<mu[3] etc).
> I know I could do this using a series of contstraints but I thought it would
> easier via sorting?

All you need is the ordered type, where

ordered[K] mu;

declares mu to be a vector in increasing order, which means

mu[1] <= mu[2] <= ... <= mu[K].

I haven't tried using it to identify a mixture model.
But now that I think about it, it may be better than
sorting because if the true values are

mu[1] = 0.5 sigma[1] = 1.5
mu[2] = 0.55 sigma[2] = 0.25
...

then you might find the first two mixture components changing
order in a posterior based on sorting, which would definitely mess
up R-hat.

> I was playing around with the mixture model in the
> Stan manual and I realized that its results are not so easily interpretable
> because any mixture component could correspond to any of the modes.

This has already come up several times on the users' list.

If you sort it out with ordering and it works, I'll revise the
section of the manual for the next release.

- Bob

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] sort [for mixture components]
parts:
On 5/1/13 10:25 PM, Marco wrote:
>
>>>> B
>>>> Do we have a sort() function or something similar in Stan?
>>> No. There's an index of functions in the very back of
>>> the manual.
>>>
>>> It is on the to-do list of functions to add :-)
>>>
> Sounds easy to with std::sort. I can do it if you wish, have anyone assigned to it already? (sorry, I couldn't find this
> function on the to-do list). Is a version for matrices also needed?

There's a section on sorting and interpolation.
But you're right --- sort() itself isn't on the list!

Issue 1 is which types it'll work for. Probably
just

real[]
int[]
vector
row_vector

We would not want it to sort in place. So you'd have
to copy to a std::vector, apply std::sort, then return
(for real[] and int[]) or use to map an Eigen vector (for
vector and row_vector).

The to-do list did have this:

-- rank(v,s): number of components of v less than v[s]
-- ranked(v,s): s-th smallest component of v

These are BUGS functions.

http://www.mrc-bsu.cam.ac.uk/bugs/winbugs/manual14.pdf

The first can be implemented
in constant memory and O(s) time. The second can be
implemented in O(s) memory and O(n log min(s,n-s)) time.

With sort(), I don't think we'd need these functions.
See this discussion on the JAGS list (JAGS uses sort()
instead of rank() and ranked()):

http://sourceforge.net/p/mcmc-jags/discussion/610037/thread/64ce3a9c

- Bob

Yes, Marco's sort and rank implementations have been
merged into our develop branch. But they won't be in
an official release until 2.0 comes out, which we are
narrowing in on.

There's nothing returning the array of indices in
sort order, but I can see where that would be useful.

Could I inquire as to the use case? It'll help motivate
us to do it and give us an example to write up.

In C++, we'd just use a pair consisting of the index
and value, sort the pairs on value, then dump out the
indices.

- Bob
